L60@P1: While employing COSTAR with both open-ended and point-of-view (POV) questions in
L61@P1: localized LLMs, we observed limitations in this technique when attempting to mimic specific
L62@P1: human response behaviors. Through experimental evaluation, we found that while COSTAR
L63@P1: improves LLM output structure and clarity, this technique is often insufficient for smaller models
L64@P1: tasked with mimicking specific human response behaviors. In such cases, the models tended to
L65@P1: return incomplete or non-committal outputs. To address this limitation, we introduce COSTARA, a novel prompt engineering framework developed in this study. COSTAR-A builds on the
L66@P1: original six COSTAR elements by incorporating a seventh component, “Answer”, which
L67@P1: explicitly instructs the model to provide an answer. This addition is particularly useful in lowresource AI scenarios where shorter output tokens are required, and model responsiveness is
L68@P1-2: crucial. The primary purpose of this study is to support the development of practical, lightweight 3
L69@P2: prompting strategies that help locally run LLMs perform more reliably in real-world
L70@P2: applications. This work contributes to the emerging body of research on structured prompting as
L71@P2: a viable alternative to retraining, post-processing, or fine-tuning, particularly for developers and
L72@P2: researchers working within resource constraints or building deployable AI agents.
L73@P2: 2. Related Work
L74@P2: 2.1 Prompt Engineering
L75@P2: Prompt engineering is the practice of crafting input instructions to guide LLMs toward producing
L76@P2: desired outputs without modifying the model’s internal parameters. The field has evolved from
L77@P2: basic direct queries to sophisticated techniques that leverage the model’s reasoning and
L78@P2: knowledge capabilities (Sahoo et al., 2025). Foundational methods include zero-shot prompting,
L79@P2: in which the model performs a task relying solely on its pre-trained knowledge without any prior
L80@P2: examples, and few-shot prompting, in which a few input-output examples are given within the
L81@P2: prompt to help guide the model’s output (Brown et al., 2020). Advanced prompting methods
L82@P2: address deeper challenges. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves logical reasoning in
L83@P2: models by encouraging step-by-step thinking, while Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
L84@P2: grounds model outputs with relevant information from an external knowledge base. Other
L85@P2: techniques, such as Self-Consistency (selecting the most consistent answer from multiple
L86@P2: generated reasoning paths) and Active Prompting (iteratively selecting the most informative
L87@P2: questions for annotation), further illustrate how prompting can actively shape model behavior
L88@P2: (Sahoo et al., 2025).
L89@P2: Designing effective prompts requires clear, specific instructions, relevant context, and often an
L90@P2: iterative process of prompt refinement (Craig et al., 2024; Kopp, 2025). Using few-shot
L91@P2: examples provides valuable guidance to the models, structuring the prompts with delimiters and
L92@P2: paying careful attention to the length of the prompt (Antoniadis, 2024; Wang et al., 2025).
L93@P2: Ultimately, a strong understanding of the specific LLM’s capabilities and limitations is essential
L94@P2: for crafting effective prompts.
L95@P2: 2.2 The COSTAR Framework
L96@P2: The COSTAR framework originated from GovTech Singapore and offers a structured
L97@P2: methodology for crafting effective prompts for LLMs that produce more relevant outputs
L98@P2: (Antoniadis, 2024). The framework breaks down the prompt design process into six key
L99@P2: components (Teo, 2023):
L100@P2: • Context: Provide background information on the task to ensure the LLM understands the
L101@P2: specific scenario being discussed.
L102@P2: • Objective: Clearly define the task you want the LLM to perform. This makes the LLM
L103@P2: focus on meeting your desired goal.
L104@P2: • Style: Specify the writing style you want the LLM to use. This could be a particular
L105@P2: famous person’s style of writing or that of an expert in a profession.
L106@P2: • Tone: Set the attitude of the output. This ensures that the LLM’s output communicates
L107@P2: the desired sentiment and emotional context.
L108@P2: • Audience: Identify the audience for whom the output is intended. This will tailor the
L109@P2: output to the audience’s understanding level.
L110@P2-3: • Response: Provide the desired output format and length. 4
L111@P3: The COSTAR framework aims to provide a systematic method for enhancing the clarity,
L112@P3: relevance, and effectiveness of LLM prompts. COSTAR’s perceived utility is further evidenced
L113@P3: by the development of tools, such as a Chrome extension for COSTAR (Doufulai, 2024). This
L114@P3: simplifies the prompt creation process for users interacting with several commonly used cloudbased LLMs.
L115@P3: This framework has been applied across various domains, including mobile app marketing,
L116@P3: technical writing, creative writing, and sentiment analysis (Antoniadis, 2024). Use cases also
L117@P3: include generating structured outputs in formats such as JSON and code (Shah, 2025), as well as
L118@P3: supporting healthcare applications like creating customized handouts and quizzes (Non, 2024).
L119@P3: 2.3 Localized Large Language Models
L120@P3: Localized LLMs are smaller, resource-efficient AI models deployed on local hardware such as
L121@P3: personal devices or private servers. While early iterations of such models were developed
L122@P3: primarily due to computational limitations in the early stages of neural network and NLP
L123@P3: research, modern localized LLMs are intentionally designed to support efficient, privacypreserving, and low-latency performance without relying on remote cloud infrastructure
L124@P3: (Nguyen, 2024). These models are sometimes smaller parameter versions of larger cloud-based
L125@P3: LLMs, designed for efficiency, or models that have been intentionally fine-tuned on specific
L126@P3: datasets to perform specialized tasks with limited computational power, memory, and energy
L127@P3: consumption (Mitra, 2025). The rise of localized LLMs reflects a broader trend toward efficient,
L128@P3: privacy-conscious AI deployments. These models offer several advantages, including enhanced
L129@P3: data privacy and security, reduced latency, enabling offline functionality, and lower operational
L130@P3: costs compared to cloud-based alternatives. Fine-tuning plays an important role in their
L131@P3: effectiveness, which allows them to outperform larger models within narrowly defined domains
L132@P3: (Mitra, 2025).
L133@P3: Applications of localized LLMs span a wide range of sectors, particularly where data sensitivity
L134@P3: or offline operation is required. They are increasingly used in coding assistance, internal
L135@P3: organizational knowledge management, web research, and report writing. Industries such as
L136@P3: healthcare, finance, education, and IoT are leveraging localized models for use cases ranging
L137@P3: from medical documentation to fraud detection and personalized learning (Nguyen, 2024). For
L138@P3: example, localized LLMs are being used to provide farmers in rural areas with immediate
L139@P3: recommendations on crop diseases (Zhu et al., 2024). Additionally, advancements in model
L140@P3: optimization have enabled the deployment of LLMs on resource-constrained devices like the
L141@P3: Raspberry Pi. Tools such as Ollama facilitate running models like Phi-2 and Mistral-7B locally
L142@P3: on Raspberry Pi 5, making AI applications more accessible and cost-effective at the edge (Kyaw,
L143@P3: 2024; Rovai, 2024). Despite these advantages, successful deployment demands careful attention
L144@P3: to hardware limitations, model size, and the implementation of optimization techniques to ensure
L145@P3: efficient performance on resource-constrained devices and environments.
L146@P3: Building upon the diverse applications of localized LLMs, there is a growing recognition of their
L147@P3: role in addressing the challenges associated with the resource-intensive nature of large-scale AI
L148@P3: models. The increasing scrutiny over the environmental and computational costs of deploying
L149@P3: expansive cloud-based models has catalyzed a shift towards more efficient, domain-specific
L150@P3: LLMs that can operate effectively on local hardware (Luccioni et al., 2024). This paradigm shift
L151@P3: is an output to resource constraints as well as an acknowledgement of the practicality and
L152@P3-4: sufficiency of smaller models in delivering targeted solutions (Yadav, 2024). 5
L153@P4: Major technology companies have begun to embrace this approach, developing models
L154@P4: optimized for local deployment on devices with limited computational resources, such as those
L155@P4: with <32GB of RAM or standard consumer-grade GPUs. This trend highlights a broader
L156@P4: industry movement towards democratizing AI capabilities, which makes them more accessible

L667@P15: strategies.
L668@P15: A major takeaway from this study is that prompt engineering alone cannot fully compensate for
L669@P15: model limitations, especially when operating under token constraints or with smaller LLMs.
L670@P15: Therefore, while COSTAR-A may not be universally effective across all localized models, it is
L671@P15: particularly useful in scenarios that require structured, human-like outputs, especially for tasks
L672@P15: involving perspective-taking or when models tend to under-respond. The framework offers the
L673@P15: most benefit when paired with localized LLMs that benefit from explicit prompting, though
L674@P15: prompt design should remain adaptable to model-specific behaviors and task demands.
L675@P15: This work was motivated by the need to support low-resource deployments of AI, specifically in
L676@P15: scenarios where developers rely on smaller models due to budget, privacy, or computational
L677@P15: limitations. In such contexts, preprocessing techniques such as structured prompting are often
L678@P15: employed to enhance output quality without requiring model retraining. However, as our
L679@P15: findings show, these improvements are often use-case-specific and do not necessarily generalize
L680@P15: across models or domains.
L681@P15: This study focused on a limited set of localized LLMs, and performance was evaluated using a
L682@P15: small number of representative questions. As such, results may not fully capture how these
L683@P15: prompting strategies behave in more complex or dynamic task environments. Additionally, token
L684@P15: limits and lack of GPU optimization may have influenced model responsiveness, particularly for
L685@P15: larger models. These factors underscore the importance of viewing prompt engineering as one
L686@P15: component within a larger system of output refinement.
L687@P15: In practice, structured prompting is only one part of generating useful outputs. Many
L688@P15: applications, especially those that require strict format adherence, data extraction, or validation,
L689@P15: will likely need post-processing. Techniques such as beam search, logit filtering, or rule-based
L690@P15: cleanup can further enhance outputs by reducing hallucinations or token artifacts (Lourenço,
L691@P15: 2024). For cases involving integration into downstream systems, a lightweight post-processing
L692@P15: step can ensure schema compliance or eliminate redundancy, increasing reliability when raw
L693@P15: model outputs fall short.
L694@P15: In summary, our results suggest that:
L695@P15: • Localized LLMs vary widely in their ability to respond meaningfully under tight token
L696@P15: limits.
L697@P15: • Structured prompts, such as COSTAR, can improve output clarity but may introduce
L698@P15: overhead that limits the completeness of outputs for certain localized LLMs.
L699@P15: • The addition of explicit output directives, as in COSTAR-A, can improve decisiveness
L700@P15: for certain models and tasks, but not all.
L701@P15: • Model sensitivity to prompt format underscores the need for careful evaluation before
L702@P15-16: adopting a single prompting strategy across systems.17
L703@P16: 6. Conclusion
L704@P16: This paper introduced COSTAR-A, a novel prompting framework designed to enhance the
L705@P16: output behavior of localized large language models (LLMs) in resource-constrained,
L706@P16: computationally efficient deployments. Building on the established COSTAR structure,
L707@P16: COSTAR-A adds an explicit “Answer” directive that encourages smaller models to produce
L708@P16: more complete and decisive outputs, particularly for point-of-view tasks where LLMs may
L709@P16: otherwise remain silent or indecisive. Our structured assessments with both open-ended and
L710@P16: multiple-choice questions showed that while COSTAR-A can meaningfully improve output
L711@P16: quality for certain localized models and tasks, the framework’s effectiveness is not universal, just
L712@P16: as COSTAR is not always superior to CAP, and outcomes vary depending on model architecture,
L713@P16: task complexity, and token limitations. These findings demonstrate the importance of designing
L714@P16: prompts that remain task- and model-specific, particularly in settings where retraining is
L715@P16: impractical. For researchers and developers working with lightweight AI agents or localized
L716@P16: models at the edge, COSTAR-A offers a practical, adaptable approach to guiding output
L717@P16: generation through prompt engineering alone, contributing both a new technique and a deeper
L718@P16: understanding of how structured input design can extend the practical capabilities of localized
L719@P16-17: LLMs for targeted, efficient, and use-case-aware deployments.18

L322@P7: 3.5.1 Part A
L323@P7: The five models were set to create a maximum of 50 new tokens in each model output, allowing
L324@P7: for comparisons across models while also setting a predefined threshold, as defined by the
L325@P7: research team. Beyond comparing the models, the team sought concise model output to address a
L326@P7: specific applied content need for the team’s future AI deployment. Deterministic sampling was
L327@P7: achieved for all models, thereby minimizing the randomness in their outputs. We did not use
L328@P7: token count as a comparative metric across models because the imposed token limit standardized
L329@P7: the length of outputs, rendering token count differences negligible for our analysis. Additionally,
L330@P7: a streamer function was employed to prevent the models from repeating the prompt in their

L339@P8: with 1 indicating a correct answer and 0 otherwise. For factual, numerical, and contextual
L340@P8: questions, correctness was based on objective accuracy. For the opinion-based and
L341@P8: summarization questions, correctness was judged on the relevance and logical coherence of the
L342@P8: output, as determined through human evaluation. Models with high correctness were prioritized.
L343@P8: Completion Time: Another important evaluation metric we used was the overall completion time
L344@P8: for all five questions. All completion time measurements were conducted on the same computing

L349@P8: finished generating its output. Models with shorter completion times while maintaining a high

L356@P8: were present. Models that consistently produced clean, direct answers without self-reference or
